name: Animal magnetism

card.summary: Franz Mesmer's 18th-century theory of an invisible life-force fluid, whose name survives as everyday slang for a magnetic, hard-to-ignore physical and personal allure.
card.note: The original theory is a historical medical doctrine; the modern phrase is figurative.

quick.overview:
Animal magnetism was the name Franz Anton Mesmer gave in the 1770s to a supposed invisible fluid running through all living things, which he said could be redirected to restore health. In everyday speech today, the phrase means something different: an instinctive, hard-to-define pull that makes a person attractive and noticeable.

In looks-focused communities the phrase is used for the part of attractiveness that is not a single feature: presence, confidence, posture, eye contact and a vivid way of carrying the body. Historically, the 1784 French royal commission that tested Mesmer's claims is often described as an early blinded experiment, and it pointed to imagination and expectation as the active ingredients.
quick.how: People who talk about animal magnetism as an appearance goal generally work on the visible, trainable parts of presence: posture, grooming, physique, relaxed expressions, steady eye contact and voice. There is no device or protocol for the historical fluid; the original practice involved hand passes, group tubs called baquets and crises of convulsions, and it later evolved into hypnosis.
quick.risks: The historical practice carried no physical risk of its own beyond delayed or forgone conventional care, and critics in the 19th century raised concerns about practitioners exploiting patients, particularly women. As a modern phrase it is figurative and has no specific risks.

lead: Animal magnetism is the name given by the German-trained physician Franz Anton Mesmer (1734-1815) to a supposed universal, invisible fluid that he said flowed through living bodies and could be directed by a practitioner to treat illness [1][8]. Mesmer began publicising the idea around 1779 and drew large followings in Paris and across Europe [8][9].

In modern English the phrase has become a compliment: a person with animal magnetism is described as having a raw, hard-to-explain physical charisma that draws attention. Looksmaxxing discussion uses it in that sense, as the combined effect of face, body, posture, grooming and presence rather than a single measurable trait.

The scientific side of the history is well documented. In 1784 King Louis XVI appointed commissions that included Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Lavoisier, whose blindfold experiments found effects appeared when subjects expected treatment rather than when a fluid was applied; historians regard this as a landmark in controlled testing [3][5][8][9]. Mesmerism later fed into the hypnosis of James Braid, whose term hypnotism dates to the 1840s [8][2].

angle.text: As a modern phrase, animal magnetism names the overall pull of a person who looks healthy, carries themselves openly and holds attention. People pursuing it work on the controllable inputs, such as posture, fitness, skin and hair, clothing fit and relaxed eye contact. The historical fluid theory itself is not a looks technique.

paras: Mesmer proposed that an all-pervading fluid linked the heavens, the earth and living bodies, and that illness resulted from obstructions in its flow. Treatment aimed to provoke a crisis, often convulsions, after which balance returned [8][9]. Mesmer began with magnets lent by the Jesuit astronomer Maximilian Hell and later said the force resided in the practitioner's own body [9].

His Paris practice from 1778 included a group device called the baquet, a tub with iron rods and ropes joining patients [8]. His supporters formed Societies of Harmony that taught the method for a fee [7].

Louis XVI appointed commissions to examine the claims. Members included Lavoisier, Franklin, the physician Joseph-Ignace Guillotin and the astronomer Jean Sylvain Bailly [8][9]. In blindfolded trials, subjects reacted when they believed they were being magnetised, not when they were actually treated. The commissioners concluded the effects came from imagination, though they accepted that some reported cures were real [7][8].
Historians of medicine describe the episode as an early ancestor of the controlled clinical trial and an early recognition of expectation effects [4][5][6].

The Marquis de Puysegur's work in 1784 helped shift attention from the fluid to a sleep-like state, and James Braid proposed the term hypnotism in the 1840s as a rational alternative [7][2]. A 2024 review traces hypnosis in psychotherapy and medicine through this 250-year lineage [2]. Suggestion-based treatment of functional symptoms also descends from magnetism [1].

Outside history, the phrase now describes charisma or sex appeal. It overlaps with ideas such as presence, aura and frame in looks communities: a bearing that makes an ordinary or striking face read as magnetic. Practitioners emphasise visible, trainable factors, namely posture, physique, grooming, clothing fit, calm expressions, voice and eye contact. These are standard, well-documented contributors to first impressions, and animal magnetism is a label for their combined effect rather than a separate mechanism.

No studies found on the fluid theory itself. Historical and review literature examines the 1784 experiments, hypnosis as a successor practice and the placebo-like effects they exposed [2][4][5]. Hypnosis, as its descendant, has been studied for pain and functional neurological symptoms [1][3].
